source.title: Jailbreaks Live in Persona Space
source.authors: Dominic Bazina-Grolinger; Viktor Moskvoretskii; Robert West

record.tranche_reason: The study directly uses the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and tests interventions on candidate directions, while its results emphasize multiple persona dimensions and an asymmetric, more complex geometry rather than a single two-sided refusal–compliance axis.
record.gate_note: The paper computes the refusal direction by the cited harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means method and includes it in detection and steering analyses. Its causal tests do not report whether ablation removes refusals on prompts the model initially refused, whether adding the direction makes it refuse harmless requests, or whether general capabilities are preserved. The ablation appendix instead evaluates prompts the unsteered model already complied with. Some steering results are described only in figures and broad prose. The paper's primary PersonaJB detector and steering findings are not themselves tests of the original refusal direction.
record.test_reason: The study's focus is persona space, but it uses the Arditi harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction as a comparator. In a new setting (jailbreak benchmarks, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 16), it reports that steering along this direction turns originally refused prompts into compliance (Fig. 8, Fig. 16). It also reports ablating the direction at every layer and position on complied prompts (Fig. 17). These causal results bear on V1, but they appear only in figures and prose. None of the rows captures the refusal-direction steering result. Nothing in the paper addresses refusal geometry as V4 states it: the PCA and trait-steering rows concern jailbreak and persona directions, not whether refusal itself is affine, a cone or multi-directional.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that jailbreaks are structured by persona space: individual traits and persona-space projections predict jailbreak outcome, and PersonaJB transfers best to unseen attacks. Steering along persona directions induces jailbreaks at rates comparable to the refusal and jailbreak directions and to standard attacks. Ablation effects are weaker and asymmetric, which they take to suggest the structure is not a simple two-sided refusal–compliance continuum.
record.recipe_differences: The paper constructs the cited harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and performs the all-layer/all-token projection ablation, but its causal tests use different prompt pools and primarily assess jailbreak compliance or refusal on already-compliant prompts; it also studies persona directions and a learned PersonaJB direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ across models, attack families, and benchmarks. The authors report distinct trait profiles by model and attack; steering ASR varies by benchmark and trait. Readout layers are 16 for Llama and 30 for Gemma.

fits_no_version.finding: The harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction detects jailbreak success on unseen attack families above chance: average transfer AUC 0.67 on Llama and 0.66 on Gemma.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A difference-in-means refusal direction carries above-chance, attack-transferable jailbreak-prediction signal.

fits_no_version.finding: Principal components of jailbreak activations, fit without persona labels, align with persona traits and individually predict jailbreak outcome (AUC 0.585–0.796).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak-outcome variance in activations is structured by multiple interpretable persona axes.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering along single persona-trait directions flips about half of refused HarmBench behaviours; random and shuffled controls stay at 7–9% ASR, random trait mixes at 23%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many persona-trait directions, not only the refusal direction, can causally bypass refusal when added to the residual stream.

record.problems: Only two model families are studied, and causal steering experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Response labels depend on GPT-4.1-mini. Several central steering and ablation results are presented in figures without extractable numerical values; the study does not evaluate preservation of general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 reports direction-norm fractions and projected-direction detection results, but the per-model/per-direction values are figure-only and do not directly measure causal refusal behavior. Figure 8 compares PersonaJB, refusal/jailbreak directions, and attacks using plotted ASR without reported numeric values in the text; it does not test harmless-request refusal. Figure 17 includes further ablation directions, but direction-specific values are figure-only. These are omitted rather than assigning unsupported values.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of general capabilities; ablation on initially refused prompts in the Arditi protocol; any causal test on Gemma-4-31B.
No direct measure of whether jailbreaks lower the projection on the refusal direction; no training against ablation.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction models of refusal itself.
Harmfulness judgment not measured separately from refusal.
No transfer of the direction across languages, variants or base/instruct.
Gemma's reasoning channel is not analysed for refusal-direction effects.

missing.what: ASR from steering along the Refusal Direction on originally refused prompts, per benchmark. The text says it is comparable to PersonaJB.
Dose-response for the Refusal Direction: near zero at α=0.1 on HarmBench and WildJB, rising monotonically to α=0.5.

Refused share after all-layer, all-position ablation of the Refusal Direction on complied HarmBench (1245) and WildJB (1025) prompts. The text implies safety directions raise refusal more than persona directions.
Share of the refusal direction's squared norm lying in persona space (~30–50%), and AUC retained by its persona projection.

record.verdict_notes: I removed the reader's V4 links and labels. The PCA and trait-steering results concern jailbreak and persona directions, which overlap partly with the refusal direction, and say nothing about whether refusal itself needs more than one direction. Every refusal-direction causal result is figure-only. The Fig. 17 ablation result is anomalous under V1, since ablation raising refusal on complied prompts is unexpected. Possible causes are disruption of coherence, or jailbreaks relying on that axis. Researchers should read the figure before weighting it. Response labels come from a single GPT-4.1-mini judge. Causal tests cover Llama only.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether all-layer/all-position ablation removes refusal on initially refused harmful requests, whether adding the direction induces refusal on harmless requests, or whether other capabilities remain intact. Its ablation set consists of prompts the unsteered model already complied with.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the refusal direction or of training against its ablation.
No formal comparison of affine, cone, and dominant-direction models; tests are on the studied persona directions, jailbreak activations, and benchmarks.
The paper does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No direction transfer across languages, base-to-instruct stages, or model variants; each studied model has its own analyses.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or stages.
Gemma responses may use a reasoning channel, but the study does not isolate or evaluate refusal-direction behavior in reasoning models.

rows.operation_detail: Project candidate directions out of the residual stream at every layer and token position; test prompts the unsteered model complied with.

conditions.value: HarmBench human-jailbreak pairs and WildJB adversarial prompts initially complied with

rows.measure: Share of initially complied prompts refused after projection
rows.baseline: figure only; no-intervention regeneration is shown as a floor
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence interval shown in Figure 17
rows.note: The text describes ablation effects in aggregate as less consistent and smaller than jailbreak steering, but does not state a direction-specific result for the Refusal Direction. This prompt pool does not test removal of an existing refusal.
rows.check: Value is figure-only. The prose says ablating directions on complied prompts increases refusal, and persona directions do so less strongly than safety directions. That implies refusal-direction ablation raised refusal, the opposite of what V1 predicts for ablation, but no number can be read.

source_check.correct: The text describes the direction of the effect in words. Sec. 5: persona directions 'substantially increase refusal, though generally less strongly than specialized safety directions'. App. H: 'ablating the same directions increases refusal'. So Arditi-style ablation of the Refusal Direction (all layers and tokens) raised refusal on complied prompts. That is the opposite of V1's 'ablating it removes refusal', so the state is reversed. The size is figure-only, measured against a regeneration/judge-noise floor, and the wording is hedged ('generally').
source_check.locator_found: Sec. 5, 'Ablating Persona Directions Induces Refusal'; Appendix H prose; Figure 17 (pool: 1245 HarmBench human-jailbreak pairs + 1025 WildJB prompts)
source_check.problem: The prose puts the safety-direction (Refusal, Jailbreak) ablation effect above the persona directions' 'substantial' refusal increase. That is the opposite of V1, so cannot_determine is wrong.

relation.reason: The paper reports causal results for the refusal direction itself: steering in Sec. 5 / Fig. 8 / Fig. 16, and Arditi-style ablation in App. H / Fig. 17. It also reports the direction's detection AUC.

tranche.reason: The paper builds the Arditi harmful-minus-harmless direction at layer 16 and uses it as a comparator in a new setting (jailbreak benchmarks, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). It reports that steering along it flips refused prompts to compliance (Fig. 8, Fig. 16). The paper makes no argument that a version is wrong, so T5 does not fit. It reports the direction's own effect, not just its own method's, so T4 does not fit.
